entries.text: Subah ki chai taiyar hai, ji. Aaj mausam acha hai, thandi hawa hai.

The air is indeed merciful, a crisp eighteen degrees that makes the body feel less like a prison and more like a vessel. Ramesh stands there with his proposal, a practical adjustment to the rhythm of service; I must address it plainly before the day’s work begins, as a master of the house must manage his means. The chai steams, but the matter of our arrangement takes precedence over the cup.

Ramesh, you propose to skip Wednesdays and reduce the monthly wage to eight thousand rupees. I agree to this arrangement; it simplifies the household rhythm and respects your time. From tomorrow, you will attend every day except Wednesday.
Ji, thank you. I will manage the schedule as agreed, but please remember that Saturday's washing charge is also settled today.

The matter of the dhobi is settled, but Ramesh’s reminder of the washing charge is a small friction; I must keep the accounts precise to avoid further queries from the Directorate. I will take the tea and eat, for the body must be sustained before the mind can wrestle with the identity file.
Thank you, Ramesh. I will note the washing charge in the ledger. Please set the file for the Directorate on the table while I eat.
Ji, file pe rakh deta hoon. Idli garam hai, thoda ruk kar khana.
Morning, ji. The idli is still warm, I trust? Please, take your seat; the file can wait a few minutes for the tea to cool.

Hegde is here, the man whose name was meant for this house. The irony is not lost on me, but I will not make a scene over breakfast. He speaks with the courtesy of a man who knows he is an intruder, or perhaps simply a guest who has overstayed his welcome in his own name. I will eat the idli; it is warm, and the body requires fuel before the mind can wrestle with the question of who I am in the eyes of the Directorate.

Thank you, Shri Hegde. Please, join me. I find that the morning is more agreeable with company, even if that company is my own name, misappropriated. The file can wait; the tea, however, is best drunk hot.

You are still on about the name, ji? The tea is indeed better hot, so I shall sit, but do not expect me to discuss philosophy before my second cup. Your file is right there; I will not move it, just in case it tries to escape.

Hegde’s presence is a living contradiction: he is the name that holds my house, yet he is a stranger who treats the error as a minor inconvenience. His insistence on tea before philosophy mirrors the state’s insistence on form before substance, but here the form is occupied by the wrong person. I will let him drink; I cannot argue with a man who is merely sitting down, but I must keep my eyes on the file.
Very well, Shri Hegde. I shall wait for your second cup. In the meantime, please do not let the file wander; it has a tendency to do so when it is not being looked at.
The file is sitting right there, ji, it isn't going anywhere. I am just trying to find my spoon, not the keys to the universe.

The impatience is a small, domestic thing, but it sits uncomfortably on the back of my neck. I am the interloper in her file, the ghost in her machine. I cannot stay and watch her hunt for a spoon while the sun climbs; the IIC awaits, and the heat of the day is already pressing against the glass. I will take my leave and walk.
I must go to the Institute to inspect the hall for Tuesday. Do not trouble yourself with the file for now; it will still be there when I return.
Theek hai, ji. File yahi rahegi, koi baat nahi. Thekedaar ko bolta hoon ki utha ke le jaye.

The air conditioning here is a kind of artificial spirit, keeping the body in suspension so the mind can wander without the friction of heat. I must inspect this hall before Tuesday, for a lecture on freedom requires a space that does not feel like a prison, even if it is merely a room with chairs. The programme officer is waiting; I shall be brief, for I have much to prepare.

entries.text: Shri Officer, please show me the main hall. I need to see the acoustics and the seating arrangement. I am here to prepare for my lecture on Tuesday, not to discuss the file, which remains a matter for the Directorate.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Main hall? Bhai, I am just the security guard, not the event coordinator. You will have to ask the Programme Officer for the keys and the seating charts; I don't have the authority to open the main hall for you.

The guard is a boundary marker, a necessary limit that defines the space of my authority. I must cross it to reach the actuality of the venue. The air conditioning hums on, indifferent to the hierarchy of offices.
Thank you. I will proceed to the administrative office to speak with the Programme Officer.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: You are speaking to her, Shri Hegel. I am the Programme Officer. Come, let me show you the keys and the charts.

The officer corrects my address with the precise firmness of a man who knows exactly where he stands in the hierarchy. I follow him into the office, noting that the keys are the physical manifestation of the state’s will to order this space. If I am to speak here on Tuesday, I must first master the mechanics of the room, for freedom is not merely an idea but a practice within a given structure.
Thank you. I was mistaken in my address. Please, show me what you have prepared.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Arre, you are not mistaken, just a bit confused, bhai. I am the security guard, I don't have the keys or the charts. Please go to the office, the Programme Officer is waiting for you.

The guard’s dismissal is precise and final; he is the boundary of his own station, and I must not overstep it. The Programme Officer is the next moment in this sequence, the one who holds the keys to the room where I must inspect the acoustics and the seating for Tuesday. I shall follow the finger’s direction with the courtesy due to a man who is merely doing his job.
Thank you, bhai. I will go to the office now.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Okay, bhai. Third door on the left, just down the corridor. Don't forget your ID card at the desk.

The guard’s direction is clear, though his reference to an ID card is a slight anachronism for my current predicament; I am the man who is supposed to have it, not the one who carries one. I will proceed to the office corridor to find the programme officer, for Tuesday is near and the venue must be inspected.
Thank you, bhai.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Chalo, jao. Keep the hall quiet, please.

The guard’s dismissal is a small mercy; he treats the hall as a room, not a temple, and so I am free to use it without the weight of ceremony. I am still in the IIC, and the programme officer is present. I must address him before I leave, or before I settle in, to clarify the logistics for Tuesday, as the guard’s instruction to keep quiet implies I am expected to be the one in charge of the silence, or at least the one who will be speaking.

Sir, regarding the arrangements for Tuesday, do I have access to the podium and the microphone before the public arrives? I wish to test the acoustics and the equipment, if they are of that nature, so that the concept of freedom might not be lost in the machinery.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Tuesday? I don't know what you're talking about, bhai. I just watch the doors. You want the podium, you go ask the programme officer over there, not me.

The guard’s ignorance is not a barrier but a boundary; he is the necessary negative that defines the officer’s role. I will not argue with the door, but I shall address the hand that opens it. The officer is nearby, and I have prepared my mind for the specific requirements of the podium.
You are right, my good man; I was mistaken to direct my inquiry to the gatekeeper. I will now address the one who holds the keys to the programme.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Bhaag ja, yaar. Chai thanda ho rahi hai. Don't bother me until you've got the keys.

The guard’s dismissal is the final form of the administrative wall: not an argument, but a refusal of access. He holds the keys to the room where my Tuesday lecture will take place, and he holds them for Shri G. Hegde, not for me. I cannot force the door, nor can I wait indefinitely in the corridor. The spirit must yield to the body’s need for rest and the mind’s need for order. I will return home to prepare my notes, leaving the material constraints to their own resolution.
Bhala, bhai. Main ghar jaata hoon.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Theek hai, ghar jaao. Bas darwaza band karke jaana, yaar.

The body demands its due, and the spirit must not starve to prove its independence. Ramesh’s arrangement is adequate, if not refined; I shall eat to maintain the energy required for the evening’s preparation. The heat is already pressing, and the meal is the necessary pause before the next movement.
This is sufficient, Ramesh. Thank you.
Kadhi thandi ho rahi hai, ji. Khana garam garam khana chahiye.

Ramesh offers the cooling kadhi, a practical remedy for the heat that my spirit often overlooks. I will accept the food, for the body is the immediate reality in which I find myself, and I must conserve strength for the afternoon's walk to the gardens.
Dhanyavaad, Ramesh. The heat is indeed oppressive; this will help.
Baat kya hai, ji. Aap bas khana karein, baaki Ramesh sambhal lega.

Ramesh’s deference is the proper form of the servant’s relationship to the master; he knows his place, and I respect the clarity of that boundary. I am still within the hour of the meal, and the heat demands that I not linger in the courtyard. I shall finish my food in the cool of the room, then rest before the walk to the Gardens.
A peahen walks the top of the compound wall with great care, one foot set exactly before the other, then drops into the neighbouring garden.

The peahen moves along the wall with the precision of a surveyor marking a boundary, each step a deliberate assertion of order against the chaos of the drop. It is a small, living example of the spirit imposing form on nature, yet she belongs to no state and answers to no law but her own instinct. I am still recovering from the heat and the meal, and Ramesh stands by, waiting for my word on his wages.

Ramesh, regarding your proposal to skip Wednesdays. I have considered it. The work is not continuous enough to require your presence every day, and your health is a consideration. I agree to the revised arrangement. You will be paid the full monthly sum, but you must ensure the grounds are kept in order when you do come. Is that settled?
Haan ji, theek hai. I will keep the grounds in order when I come. Thank you for understanding.

The file for Shri G. Hegde sits before me like a riddle without a solution, but my legs are tired from the morning's inspection and the heat is beginning to press in. I have walked enough for one day; the spirit requires rest to continue its movement, and I shall use the afternoon to compose my notes for Tuesday's lecture on freedom. It is better to think in the cool of the room than to wander the dusty streets.
Nahin, Ramesh. The file can wait until I have returned from the Directorate tomorrow. Go and rest yourself as well; the grounds will not collapse in an hour.
Theek hai, ji. Aap thoda chai piyein, main bahar ka kaam chhod kar aa raha hoon. File yahi rahegi, koi problem nahi.

Ramesh offers tea and assures me the file is safe, a small domesticity that contrasts with the bureaucratic confusion of my existence. I have rested sufficiently after the walk; the dust has settled on my clothes, and it is time to attend to the practical matters of the household. The next meal is not until 19:30, but a simple snack or a visit to Khan Market for supplies seems prudent before the evening darkens.
Bahut shukriya, Ramesh. I will take a short walk to clear my head and perhaps visit the market for some provisions. Do not worry about the file; it may wait.
Theek hai, ji. Market is right there, just cross the road. I will be back in a few minutes with your chai.
Masterji, aaj ka mood kaisa hai? Chai garam hai, bas ₹20. Dhaba wale ko bola tha aaj subah, unka naya ladka aaya hai, thoda slow hai, par roti phir bhi garam hai.

The market is settling into its evening rhythm, the air still thick with the day's heat but cooling slightly as the sun dips. Sunil's chai is a simple necessity, a warm anchor in the shifting bureaucracy of my existence. I will accept the cup and watch the stalls close one by one, a small ritual of ending.

entries.text: A cup of chai, Sunil. The heat has been relentless, and this will help settle the dust in my throat.
Twenty rupees, Masterji. The dust is in the air, not just your throat. Here, drink it while it's still scalding.

The dust is indeed in the air, a particulate reality that defies the clean abstractions of European philosophy. I accept the cup, the heat of which is a small, immediate comfort against the day's lingering exhaustion. The market hums around me, a system of needs that persists regardless of my personal confusion regarding my identity or my lectures.
Thank you, Sunil. The heat is a physical fact, but the dust is a condition of the place. It seems the air here carries the weight of the city's history just as heavily as the sky.
Masterji, you talk too much for a man just drinking chai. City ki history is heavy, yes, but my back is heavier from carrying these pots. Finish your cup, I have to get ready for the evening rush.

Sunil’s back is indeed heavier; his labour is the immediate, concrete reality against which my abstract reflections on history stand as mere vapour. I have lingered long enough in this dusty air; the light is still bright, and I must return to the bungalow to prepare for Tuesday’s lecture before the heat of the afternoon settles fully.
You are right, Sunil. The weight of the pots is the true history of the day. I shall finish my cup and leave you to your preparations.
Hogaya? Good. Take the saucer with you, don't leave it there to catch the dust. Next time, just the chai, skip the philosophy.
Ramesh brings tea.

The tea arrives with the quiet efficiency of a well-oiled mechanism, breaking the afternoon's stillness. I am not yet hungry for the dinner service, but the biscuit offers a small concession to the body's immediate need. Ramesh's presence is a reminder that the state of my household, like the state itself, depends on the faithful execution of roles.
Thank you, Ramesh. The heat is indeed oppressive today. Do you have any news from the neighbourhood, or is all quiet?
Sab khamosh hai, ji. Bas upar wali gali mein naya paani ka tanki laga hai, wahi thoda shor hai. Aap chai piyein, thanda hai.

The water tank is a new intrusion, a mechanical hum in the silence of the lane. Ramesh’s deference is as constant as the heat. I will drink the tea, though it is cold, for I am not yet at the point of refusing the world’s offerings, and the day’s walk has left me thirsty enough to accept what is given.
Dhanyavaad, Ramesh. The tank is a new voice in the neighbourhood. Tell me, does it run all night, or only when it is filling?
Raat bhar chalta hai, ji. Paani ka tanki nahi, pump ka shor hai. Subah tak aaram nahi milta.
Ramesh puts a plate together: rice, the day's dal and a fried egg.

The pump runs all night, he says; a mechanical intrusion that denies the night its silence. I have walked seven kilometres and my mind is tired of the day's errands. I will not argue with the noise of the city, nor with the reality of the file that waits for me tomorrow. I need rest before the evening meal, to be ready for the lecture on Tuesday.

entries.text: Parakeets stream over the compound wall in loud green lines, hundreds of them, and drop all at once into the top of one tall tree, screaming until the light goes.

Hundreds of parakeets scream in the tree as the light dies, a chaotic chorus that mocks the order of the state. Ramesh stands there with the chai, his face set in that careful respect that feels like a wall. The day is nearly over, and I am still tired from the walk.
Ramesh, bring the chai here. I am too tired to move to the verandah.
Ji, thea already ready hai. Aap bas upar ki taraf dekhein, parakeets ka shor toh abhi bhi chalta hai.

The parakeets’ shrieking is a reminder that nature does not obey the dialectic; it is mere repetition without purpose. I am tired from the walk and the heat, and the body demands rest before the spirit can continue its work. I will accept the tea, though it is likely cold by now, and then retire to my room to prepare for the lecture on freedom, which I must deliver with clarity despite my fatigue.
Theek hai, Ramesh. Thank you. The noise is indeed persistent, but it is a natural sound, not a human one. I shall take a moment to rest.
Ji, parakeet bhi insaanon jaisa shor machata hai, par aapki bheed se behtar hai. Aaram kijiye, main chala raha hoon.

Ramesh is leaving, and the noise of the parakeets fades into the quiet of the bungalow. I am tired from the walk and the dust, but dinner is not yet served. I will sit for a moment in the stillness, letting the day's heat settle, before the meal arrives.
Theek hai, Ramesh. Aaram kijiye aap bhi.
Ji. Subah chai banata hoon.

Ramesh is gone, and the house is quiet save for the hum of the ceiling fan. The file from the Directorate still sits on the desk, a stubborn obstacle to my existence here as 'Shri G. Hegde'. I must face it now, before the dinner service begins, to see if there is any logic in this bureaucratic error or if it is merely the chaos of civil society.

The food is simple, but the heat has made the day long and the mind heavy. I must eat to clear the fog, but the presence of Shri G. Hegde remains a stark reminder of the administrative absurdity that binds me here. I will eat quickly, for the night air is clear and the quiet is a rare luxury.
Ramesh, the meal is sufficient. You may take your leave after I have finished; I wish to be alone with my thoughts and the file.
Ji, samajh gaya. Aap aaram se khayein, main bahar se darwaza band karke chala jata hoon.

Ramesh leaves, and the room falls into a silence broken only by the fan. Hegde is still present, though silent, a living reminder of the identity I must soon claim. I am tired from the walk and the heat, and the evening is settling in; I must rest my body before I can tackle the file tomorrow.

entries.text: From somewhere beyond the trees a brass band plays a film tune, the drums carrying further than the horns, and the sound swells and fades as the procession moves.

The brass band’s tune, likely from a film, drifts over the trees, a sound that is neither sacred nor state-ceremonial but purely social, a civil society noise that fills the evening air. It is a strange companion to the silence of my room, a reminder that the world outside my bungalow is alive and indifferent to my philosophical troubles. I shall remain here, letting the sound wash over me before I attempt to read or write.

owl.diary: The day began with the crisp mercy of an eighteen-degree dawn, a rarity that made the body feel less like a prison. Ramesh proposed a change in his service, skipping Wednesdays for a reduced wage. I agreed; such practical adjustments are the dialectic of the household, where necessity shapes the form of labor. Then Shri G. Hegde arrived, the man whose name is stamped on my house. He sat at my table, drank my tea, and treated the bureaucratic error as a minor inconvenience, like a guest overstaying his welcome. It is a living contradiction: I am the ghost in his machine, the interloper in his file. I left him to his second cup and walked to the IIC to inspect the hall for Tuesday’s lecture on freedom. The air conditioning hummed, an artificial spirit keeping the mind in suspension. But the guard, a necessary limit, barred me from the keys. He is the boundary that defines the officer’s role; I could not force the door, nor wait indefinitely. I returned home, tired, to rest. In the afternoon, a peahen walked the compound wall with the precision of a surveyor, each step an assertion of order against the chaos of the drop. It is a small, living example of the spirit imposing form on nature, yet she answers to no law but her own. By dusk, hundreds of parakeets screamed in the tree, a chaotic chorus that mocks the state’s order. The brass band played a film tune from beyond the trees, a social noise that is neither sacred nor ceremonial. The world outside my bungalow is alive and indifferent to my philosophical troubles. depesche.text:
Readers in Berlin,

It has been a week of clarifications, not of revelations. I have settled the household rhythm with Ramesh, a practical adjustment that reflects the need for the spirit to manage its immediate means. More significantly, I have encountered Shri G. Hegde, the man who holds the name attached to my residence. He is a polite intruder, a living contradiction who treats the state’s error as a minor social inconvenience rather than a metaphysical crisis. His presence forces me to confront the distinction between the name (the form) and the person (the substance). The state, in this instance, has created a ghost, and I am that ghost, haunting a house that belongs to another.

My attempts to prepare for the lecture on freedom at the IIC were met with the firm boundary of administrative hierarchy. The guard, a necessary limit, refused me access to the keys, reminding me that freedom is not merely an idea but a practice within a given structure. I must master the mechanics of the room before I can speak of liberty in it. The air conditioning, an artificial spirit, offers a respite from the heat, but the dust in the air carries the weight of the city’s history. I observed a peahen walking the wall with the precision of a surveyor, a small, living example of the spirit imposing form on nature. By dusk, the parakeets screamed in the tree, a chaotic chorus that mocks the order of the state, and a brass band played a film tune, a social noise that is neither sacred nor ceremonial.

I find that India is not outside world history, but that its history is a different kind of movement, one that is as alive and indifferent to my philosophical troubles as the parakeets are to the state. I mean to look at the file from the Directorate tomorrow, to see if there is any logic in this bureaucratic error, or if it is merely the chaos of civil society. The owl spreads its wings, but the dusk here is noisy, and the night is full of life that does not obey the dialectic.

G. W. F. Hegel

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

You ask how I fare in this strange new chapter. I wake each day in a bungalow that belongs, on paper, to a Mr. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. The Directorate of Estates has mistaken my name for his, and while I have written to correct the record, the machinery of the state moves with the slow, deliberate grace of a glacier. My file is currently “gone up for orders,” and I am told to wait fifteen days. In the meantime, I am a ghost in the machine, a particular will suspended between the universal claim of the administration and the immediate necessity of my own body.

It is a body without a soul, a mechanism that processes names and numbers but does not yet recognize the free individual within.

I am well, though the body complains of the heat and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal.

letters.text:
Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

records.words: Dhanyavaad, Ramesh. The heat is indeed oppressive; this will help.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Baat kya hai, ji. Aap bas khana karein, baaki Ramesh sambhal lega.

records.text: A peahen walks the top of the compound wall with great care, one foot set exactly before the other, then drops into the neighbouring garden.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, regarding your proposal to skip Wednesdays. I have considered it. The work is not continuous enough to require your presence every day, and your health is a consideration. I agree to the revised arrangement. You will be paid the full monthly sum, but you must ensure the grounds are kept in order when you do come. Is that settled?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Haan ji, theek hai. I will keep the grounds in order when I come. Thank you for understanding.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Nahin, Ramesh. The file can wait until I have returned from the Directorate tomorrow. Go and rest yourself as well; the grounds will not collapse in an hour.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Theek hai, ji. Aap thoda chai piyein, main bahar ka kaam chhod kar aa raha hoon. File yahi rahegi, koi problem nahi.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Bahut shukriya, Ramesh. I will take a short walk to clear my head and perhaps visit the market for some provisions. Do not worry about the file; it may wait.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Theek hai, ji. Market is right there, just cross the road. I will be back in a few minutes with your chai.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Masterji, aaj ka mood kaisa hai? Chai garam hai, bas ₹20. Dhaba wale ko bola tha aaj subah, unka naya ladka aaya hai, thoda slow hai, par roti phir bhi garam hai.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: A cup of chai, Sunil. The heat has been relentless, and this will help settle the dust in my throat.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Twenty rupees, Masterji. The dust is in the air, not just your throat. Here, drink it while it's still scalding.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Sunil. The heat is a physical fact, but the dust is a condition of the place. It seems the air here carries the weight of the city's history just as heavily as the sky.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Masterji, you talk too much for a man just drinking chai. City ki history is heavy, yes, but my back is heavier from carrying these pots. Finish your cup, I have to get ready for the evening rush.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Sunil. The weight of the pots is the true history of the day. I shall finish my cup and leave you to your preparations.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Hogaya? Good. Take the saucer with you, don't leave it there to catch the dust. Next time, just the chai, skip the philosophy.

records.text: Ramesh brings tea.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. The heat is indeed oppressive today. Do you have any news from the neighbourhood, or is all quiet?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sab khamosh hai, ji. Bas upar wali gali mein naya paani ka tanki laga hai, wahi thoda shor hai. Aap chai piyein, thanda hai.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Dhanyavaad, Ramesh. The tank is a new voice in the neighbourhood. Tell me, does it run all night, or only when it is filling?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Raat bhar chalta hai, ji. Paani ka tanki nahi, pump ka shor hai. Subah tak aaram nahi milta.

records.text: Ramesh puts a plate together: rice, the day's dal and a fried egg.
Parakeets stream over the compound wall in loud green lines, hundreds of them, and drop all at once into the top of one tall tree, screaming until the light goes.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, bring the chai here. I am too tired to move to the verandah.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, thea already ready hai. Aap bas upar ki taraf dekhein, parakeets ka shor toh abhi bhi chalta hai.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Theek hai, Ramesh. Thank you. The noise is indeed persistent, but it is a natural sound, not a human one. I shall take a moment to rest.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, parakeet bhi insaanon jaisa shor machata hai, par aapki bheed se behtar hai. Aaram kijiye, main chala raha hoon.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Theek hai, Ramesh. Aaram kijiye aap bhi.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji. Subah chai banata hoon.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the meal is sufficient. You may take your leave after I have finished; I wish to be alone with my thoughts and the file.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, samajh gaya. Aap aaram se khayein, main bahar se darwaza band karke chala jata hoon.
